key_terms.meaning: A complete central processing unit built on a single integrated circuit chip; it needs external memory and I/O to work.
One chip holding a CPU, memory, timers and I/O ports, designed to run a fixed program inside a product.
The part of a computer that fetches instructions, decodes them, does arithmetic and logic, and controls the rest of the system.
The number of bits the CPU handles in one operation, such as 8, 16, 32 or 64; it sets the size of registers and usually of the data bus.
A computer built into a device to do one dedicated job, such as a washing machine controller or a fuel-injection unit.
A single chip that contains a processor core plus memory, timers, and peripherals such as serial ports and converters.
A shared group of wires carrying a set of related signals between the CPU, memory and I/O; only one device may drive it at a time.
The unidirectional lines that carry the address the CPU wants; with n lines it can select 2ⁿ locations.
The lines carrying command and status signals such as READ, WRITE, clock and interrupt request.
A small, fast storage element inside the CPU holding one word, used for operands, addresses or status bits.
The CPU block that performs addition, subtraction, AND, OR, shift and comparison, and sets the flag bits.
An arrangement where I/O registers share the same address space as memory, so ordinary load and store instructions access them.
Keeping program instructions and data in the same memory, so the CPU can fetch and execute them one after another.
A machine with one memory holding both instructions and data, reached by a single set of address and data buses.
A machine with separate program and data memories and separate buses, so an instruction and an operand can be fetched in the same cycle.
Complex instruction set computer: hardware provides many powerful, variable-length instructions so a program needs fewer of them.
Reduced instruction set computer: a small set of fixed-length, register-based instructions that pipelines and compilers handle well.
The ordering of storage from fast, small, costly registers and cache down to slow, large, cheap disk and tape.
Splitting instruction execution into stages and overlapping different instructions in different stages to raise throughput.
A situation that stops the next instruction from running in its scheduled pipeline stage, caused by data, control or structural conflicts.

takeaways: A microprocessor is a CPU alone on a chip; a microcontroller is a CPU plus memory, timers and ports on the same chip.
Microprocessors evolved by shrinking transistors and widening the word from 4 bits to 8, 16, 32 and 64 bits.
Every computer transfers data over an address bus, a data bus and a control bus, and the CPU drives the sequence.
The stored-program concept lets instructions sit in memory beside data, which is what makes a general-purpose computer possible.
Von Neumann shares one memory for code and data; Harvard separates them, trading cost for speed.
CISC reduces program size by making instructions powerful; RISC reduces instruction work so pipelining and compilers stay simple.
Memory is organised as a hierarchy because no single technology is fast, large and cheap at the same time.
Pipelining raises throughput but never reduces the latency of one instruction, and hazards limit the real gain.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a labelled block diagram with a clear signal-by-signal explanation, and comparison questions (microprocessor vs microcontroller, von Neumann vs Harvard, CISC vs RISC) are almost always asked in table form.

bank.q: Define a microprocessor and a microcontroller. Compare them on at least six points, including hardware present on chip, typical clock speed, cost, power, bit width and typical application.
outline: Definitions of both terms
On-chip memory, timers, I/O ports present in a microcontroller but not a microprocessor
Instruction set and addressing modes tuned for control
Bit width and clock frequency ranges
Board-level part count and cost
Applications: general-purpose computer vs washing machine, microwave, motor controller

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a general-purpose computer showing CPU, memory and I/O, and explain the role of the address bus, data bus and control bus.
outline: Block diagram with CPU, memory, input and output blocks
Address bus: unidirectional, carries the location, n lines give 2ⁿ locations
Data bus: bidirectional, width equals the word size
Control bus: READ, WRITE, clock, reset, interrupt request and acknowledge
Timing: address placed, then read or write strobe, then data transfer
Why a bus is shared and how only one driver is enabled at a time

bank.q: Explain the stored-program concept and describe the fetch-decode-execute cycle with the registers involved.
outline: Instructions and data held in the same memory
Program counter holds the next address
Fetch: address to memory, instruction into the instruction register
Decode: control unit interprets the opcode
Execute: operands read, ALU acts, result written, flags updated
Program counter updated, cycle repeats; interrupts checked at the boundary

bank.q: Compare von Neumann and Harvard architectures with block diagrams, and state where each is used.
outline: One memory versus separate program and data memories
Single bus versus separate buses, hence simultaneous instruction and operand fetch
Von Neumann bottleneck and its effect on speed
Harvard uses more pins and silicon area
Von Neumann in general-purpose computers, Harvard in most microcontrollers and DSPs
Modified Harvard in chips with separate caches

bank.q: Explain the memory hierarchy with respect to speed, size and cost per bit, and state the principle of locality that justifies it.
outline: Order: registers, cache, main memory, secondary storage
Access time increasing down the hierarchy
Capacity increasing and cost per bit falling down the hierarchy
Locality of reference: temporal and spatial
Cache keeps recently used blocks close to the CPU
Trade-off between speed and cost drives the design

bank.q: A memory chip is specified as 2K × 8. How many address lines and data lines does it have? How many such chips are needed for an 8K × 8 memory, and how is each chip selected?
outline: 2K = 2048 = 2¹¹, so 11 address lines
8 data lines because the word is 8 bits
8K/2K = 4 chips in the word direction
Two high-order address lines feed a 2-to-4 decoder
Each decoder output drives one chip-select pin
Address map showing the range of each chip

bank.q: Describe, step by step, what the control unit does to execute a single instruction held in memory, and list the control signals it must assert for a memory read.
outline: Address from program counter onto the address bus
Memory read asserted; data strobe waits for access time
Instruction latched into the instruction register
Opcode decoded into a sequence of control steps
Operands fetched if needed
ALU operation, result written back, flags updated
Write cycle signals: address, data, WRITE strobe

bank.q: A five-stage pipeline has stages of 2 ns, 2 ns, 3 ns, 2 ns and 2 ns. Find the clock period, the time for one instruction and the throughput for a long stream of instructions. Explain why the gain is less than five.
outline: Clock period set by the slowest stage: 3 ns
One instruction still takes 5 cycles = 15 ns in steady state
Throughput approaches one instruction per 3 ns
Ideal speedup limited by the slowest stage, not the average
Pipeline fill and drain overhead
Hazards and stalls reduce the practical gain

bank.q: A washing machine controller must read a water-level sensor, a door switch and a start button, and drive a motor relay and a display. Show how these are connected to an 8-bit microcontroller, and state whether memory-mapped or isolated I/O suits this and why.
outline: Inputs and outputs listed and assigned to port pins
Each port pin as one bit; direction register set for input or output
Sensor and switch need pull-up or conditioning
Relay driven through a transistor and diode, display through a driver
Memory-mapped I/O lets ordinary instructions access ports
Isolated I/O needs special IN and OUT instructions and separate control lines

bank.q: A payment terminal must be built for a shop counter, and the team argues between an 8-bit microcontroller with on-chip flash and a microprocessor with external ROM and RAM. Evaluate both choices for cost, board size, power, expandability and design effort, and recommend one.
outline: Microcontroller: single chip, on-chip flash, RAM, timers, serial port, small board and low cost
Microprocessor: needs external memory, latch and decoder, larger board
Power: microcontroller lower, suits battery backup
Expandability: microprocessor better for large memory and graphics
Design effort and time to market favour the microcontroller
Recommendation for a fixed-function terminal, with justification

bank.q: RISC instructions are simple and CISC instructions are powerful, yet measured code size and execution time differ by far less than early claims suggested. Analyse why.
outline: CISC: fewer instructions per task but variable length and multi-cycle execution
RISC: more instructions per task but each is short and pipelined
Memory and compiler effects: register allocation, instruction scheduling
RISC needs more instructions and so more code bytes; CISC needs microcode
Modern CISC cores decode complex instructions into RISC-like micro-operations
Both ends up with similar pipelines and similar performance

bank.q: A pipeline gives a large throughput gain in theory but much less in practice. Analyse data, control and structural hazards with one example each, and state how each is reduced.
outline: Data hazard: instruction needs a result still in the pipeline
Fix by forwarding, or by stalling and inserting bubbles
Control hazard: branch target known only after fetch
Fix by branch prediction, delayed branch slot, or flushing
Structural hazard: two instructions need the same unit in one cycle
Fix by separate instruction and data memories or by duplicating hardware
Effect on speedup compared with the ideal n-stage gain

bank.q: Explain why most microcontrollers use a Harvard-style memory arrangement while general-purpose computers use a von Neumann view with separate caches.
outline: Microcontroller code is fixed in flash and data in RAM; two memories exist anyway
Separate buses allow simultaneous fetch of instruction and operand
No cache needed, so cost and predictability stay good
General-purpose computers run changing programs and need one uniform address space
Caches give speed while keeping the programmer's von Neumann model
Modified Harvard: split first-level caches, single main memory

glossary.def: A central processing unit fabricated on one integrated circuit chip, requiring external memory and I/O devices.
A single chip containing a CPU, program and data memory, timers, and input/output ports for embedded control.
The processor block that fetches, decodes and executes instructions and controls the rest of the system.
The number of bits a processor handles as one unit, fixing register size and normally the data bus width.
A computer dedicated to one control task inside a larger product.
An integrated circuit combining a processor core with memory and peripherals.
A shared set of wires with a defined protocol for transferring addresses, data or control signals.
Unidirectional lines carrying the location being read or written; n lines address 2ⁿ locations.
Bidirectional lines carrying the value transferred between the CPU and memory or I/O.
Lines that carry timing and command signals such as read, write, clock, reset and interrupt.
The set of all addresses a processor can generate, determined by the number of address lines.
A small fast storage location inside the CPU holding one word of data or an address.
The arithmetic logic unit, which performs arithmetic and logical operations and sets the flags.
A single status bit such as zero, carry, sign or overflow, set by the ALU and tested by branch instructions.
A scheme in which I/O registers occupy addresses in the same space as memory and are accessed by ordinary instructions.
A scheme in which I/O devices have a separate address space reached only by special instructions.
The principle that instructions are held in memory as binary codes and fetched like data.
A design with one memory and one bus set shared by instructions and data.
A design with physically separate program and data memories and buses.
A design philosophy using many complex, variable-length instructions to shorten programs.
A design philosophy using few simple fixed-length instructions to make pipelining and compilation easy.
Overlapping the stages of several instructions so that one instruction finishes per clock in steady state.
A dependency or resource conflict that prevents an instruction from issuing in its scheduled cycle.
The layered arrangement of storage from fast small registers to slow large secondary memory.
Logic that turns high-order address bits into chip-select signals so each device answers only its own range.
